title: Leaving without a troponin
topic: A colleague's error or poor performance
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in the Emergency Department. You notice Mr Ellis, 58, putting on his coat to leave. Glancing at his notes, you see a locum doctor recorded central chest pain radiating to his left arm this morning and a normal ECG, and discharged him. No troponin was taken.

The locum is with another patient nearby.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Tell Mr Ellis that the locum has made a mistake.
options.brief: Undermines a colleague before you know the facts.
options.detailed: There may be a reason, and saying this could alarm Mr Ellis and damage trust in the department.

options.text: Let Mr Ellis go, and arrange for him to be called back if a troponin is needed.
options.brief: Recalling him may take hours, and he may be at risk.
options.detailed: Recall systems exist, but if he is having a heart attack, he needs to be in hospital now. Letting him go is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Speak to the locum about the missing troponin.
options.brief: He may have a reason, or may realise it was missed.
options.detailed: The locum may have a clinical reason, or may have overlooked it. Asking him directly and respectfully is the quickest way to resolve it.

options.text: Ask Mr Ellis to wait while you check his plan.
options.brief: Stops him leaving before the question is answered.
options.detailed: A normal ECG doesn't rule out a heart attack, and a troponin is usually needed with this history. Asking him to wait, without alarming him, keeps him safe while you check.

options.text: Discuss it with the ED consultant in charge.
options.brief: Appropriate if the locum isn't available or disagrees.
options.detailed: The consultant can review the plan. It ranks third because asking the locum first is quicker and fairer.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you act on a possible omission by a colleague to keep a patient safe, while treating the colleague fairly.
explanation.keyDetails: Mr Ellis is leaving. His history suggests possible acute coronary syndrome. No troponin was taken. The locum is nearby.
explanation.reasoning: [D] keeps him safe, [C] asks the locum, and [E] escalates. [A] undermines a colleague without the facts, and [B] lets him leave at risk.
explanation.competing: This is hard because [D] and [C] would happen almost together. The key puts stopping him first because once he's left, it's much harder to put right. [B] ranks last because letting a possible heart attack go home carries the greatest risk; [A] is unprofessional, but at least he stays in the department.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, acting when patients may be at risk because of a colleague's decision.
